subtopic: FELICITATIONS EXTENDED ON BEHALF OF MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a year ago to-day, at the first of our morning sittings, I had the pleasure of extending to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) my best wishes and those of all hon. members of the house on the celebration of another birthday anniversary. This morning I should like to renew those good wishes and, if I may be permitted to do so, to renew them not only on my own behalf biut on behalf of all hon. members of the House of Commons.
During the last year my right hon. friend has had I think, his full share of trials and joys. Perhaps the greatest of the former has been the serious impairment of his health in that period of time. I wish him nothing more sincerely and nothing better to-day than that in the year on which he has just entered his health may be fully restored and that he may have before him many years of service to his country and great public causes.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FELICITATIONS EXTENDED ON BEHALF OF MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have so many matters to think of in these days that I have very little opportunity to think of the coming and going of birthdays. I realize that I am passing another milestone to-day and I am very grateful to the right hon. gentleman for the terms in which he has referred to my having reached another birthday. I think I can say with some frankness what most of the members of this house must realize, that the last five birthdays have not brought .me any very great joy an'd that if the high expectations of those who sit opposite are realized my next birthday will be much happier. On the other hand, however, it well might be that the birthdays of some others may not be as joyful if that event should happen.
The greatest joy that I have had, coloured as recent days have been by sadness and sorrow, has arisen from the thought that in my older age I have been able to render what some may not regard as useful service but at least some service to a country that has done so very much for me. I am conscious also-

Questions
yesterday perhaps more than I ever have been-of my impairment of health and strength, not in the general physical sense but because of the condition of my heart, which does not permit me to participate to the extent I should like in what may foe called the rough and tumble of parliamentary life.
I am grateful to my colleagues and those who sit on this side of the house for this beautiful basket of flowers, which contains all too many roses, and to the right hon. gentleman and those who sit around him for the kind terms in which he has referred to my having reached another milestone in life's journey. Whether or not we are privileged to meet together on another occasion to celebrate an event so auspicious remains for time to disclose.

The house resumed from Thursday, June 27, consideration in committee of Bill No. 120, for the purpose of establishing in Canada a system of long-term mortgage credit for fishermen-Mr. Stirling-Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 6-Conditions for loans.

Mr. Chairman, where will we get the money for this purpose? During the campaign of 1930 the right hon. Prime Minister said there would be reforms in taxation. When the last government was in power more taxation was possible. In 1933, according to press reports, the Prime Minister stated that Canada was near the limit of her credit, and in the following year, 1934 after imposing heavy taxation he said that Canada had reached the limit of her credit. Therefore I say that is ample proof that the government has exhausted Canada's credit. That is all I have to say. I do not see how they can get more money.

I find myself more or less in sympathy with the objects behind the bill, and particularly is that true of hon. members representing shore fishermen. Hon. members from constituencies adjoining fishing grounds must be well aware of the desperate condition under which fishermen are living. But those of us who know the particular requirements of fishermen cannot, I fear, get very much hope from any of the provisions in the bill. Our fishermen do

Mortgage Credits jor Fishermen
not require any large amount of money. All that the boat fisherman needs is a small amount, possibly S50, S75 or $100 at the beginning of the fishing season so that' he may fit out his boat, gear and other equipment. They require, further, a ready market for their product.
In a cumbersome way this bill seeks to deal with a very simple question. Of course there is no doubt that under the provisions of the bill a large amount of money could be raised, but it is when we come to the distribution of the money among the fishermen that I see great difficulty so far as possible benefits are concerned. Evidently the bill is drafted along the lines of the farm loan legislation. Those of us who have studied the matter do not believe that the farm loan board is adapted to provide money for fishermen and the machinery set up by that board cannot be used to their advantage.
I repeat that this bill provides only a very cumbersome method of financing, and the fishermen I represent are not in a position to avail themselves of its provisions. Any fisherman who has security sufficient to enable him to comply with the provisions of the act would not have to avail himself of those provisions. He could secure any financial assistance he required either through the banks or through private agencies. Then, there is no provision in the bill for marketing. My view is that if by more simple means we can attain the objects sought by the fishermen there is no necessity for the cumbersome method provided in this measure. The ordinary fisherman wants fifty or seventy-five or a hundred dollars in the spring, and that is all he wants. That enables him to secure his boat, fix up his nets and get his plant. There should also be some provision for insurance against the loss of his little plant, which everybody knows is quite apt to happen because of the hazardous nature of the fisherman's calling. We used to have a very simple method of assisting farmers in the purchase of their seed in the spring. An amount of money was provided and placed in the hands of a responsible party who advanced seventy-five or one hundred dollars to the farmer, taking his notes, and repayment being made when the harvest came in the fall. There is no reason why such a procedure could not be adopted in dealing with the fishermen, and particularly the boat fishermen of whom I speak. I do not wish to delay the house. All I want to do is to go on record as expressing with some reluctance my own view which is that this bill will not be of any assistance to the fishermen I have the honour to represent in this house.

I rise to say just a word or two in regard to this bill. I do not think I can add very much to what the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. MacDonald, Cape Breton) has said. I have been disappointed in the provisions of the bill in so far as they appear to be cumbersome. The particular feature which has given me concern is that this bill makes as a sine qua non, a condition precedent to the fisherman getting the benefit of the loan, the possession of real estate. Now among the fishermen with whom I am acquainted, generally speaking if a man has a house and lot free of any encumbrances so that he can give a first mortgage on it, he probably will not find very much difficulty in getting whatever credit is necessary in order to purchase a boat or to purchase gear. It seems to me that the bill misses entirely the essential, that the security should 'be in connection with the property which is being purchased, in connection with the facilities that are being required.
I thoroughly agree with the desirability for something of this kind. I have brought to the attention of the house and the attention of the minister on more than one occasion the necessities of the fishermen, particularly those who have lost their gear on account of unusual storms. These men find themselves with earning capacity, with willingness to work, with ability to work, but without capital and in some instances they are young men who have no property of any kind, while in other cases they may be married men whose property is mortgaged in so far as it can be mortgaged for previous obligations. That is why we have to damn this bill with faint praise. That is why I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South has found it necessary to take the stand he did. I am going to support this bill. I will do anything I can to heLp make it a success, but I feel that it puts a fundamental barrier in the way of a fisherman getting the assistance that he needs when it required that in order to get the benefit of the law he mu^t have real estate, and real estate free so that he can give a first mortgage upon it.
I agree with my hon. friend that the amount the fisherman requires is not large. My hon. friend mentioned seventy-five or one hundred dollars, but I have known fishermen to want three or four hundred dollars. The boat builder will give a man some credit if he has property, but if the government will not trust him unless he has property the boat builder can hardly be expected to do so. It is the same with regard to gear lost on account of storms. We have had terrible storms on the south coast of Nova Scotia in the last year

Mortgage Credits jor Fishermen
with a tremendous loss of gear, leaving fishermen simply strapped, and there is no possibility of insurance such as a man would have in connection with a house or store or factory if destroyed by fire. These men are left absolutely to shift for themselves, and the only way they can get a living is by going shares in somebody else's boat. Naturally they can make very much more themselves by fishing independently, and naturally it means the production of fish is cut off to that extent.
I do feel that the bill lacks the assistance which should be provided for a most deserving class. I cannot forbear saying that in view of what is being done along some other lines I feel that a bill more generous in its terms, more easily applicable, more simple in its administration, and one which would impose less requirements on the fishermen,, could have been devised than the one before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I indicated on a previous occasion the difficulties connected with granting loans to the participants in any industry are great. The government has given a great deal of consideration to this endeavour. Is it desirable or not that loans of small amounts should be granted to fishermen? It is decided that it is desirable to do so within certain limits. The question immediately arises, what shall the security be? The government has decided that it will go so far as to offer fishermen provisions similar to those which have been granted for some years to the farmer, but that is as far as the government thinks it wise to go.
It has been suggested that the machinery which would have to be made use of is cumbersome. Well, the machinery has been set up. It has been in use for the farmers for a considerable number of years. It has been somewhat simplified by the amending bill of this year, and it is thought that with that machinery, with a chief executive officer in each province now who will represent the views of the Canadian farm loan board sitting at Ottawa, with the assistance of a loan advisory committee in the locality whose chairman shall be that chief executive officer, and associated with them shall be those from the locality and consequently knowledgeable in this matter, it should not be cumbersome in its operation. But this is as far as the government proposes to go.

I just want to say that
I think the minister has missed the point entirely when he says that we are doing the same thing for the fisherman as we have done for the farmer. The farmer by the very

nature of his calling has a piece of land which he can mortgage, but the fisherman may not have a piece of land at all, no more than he may have a diamond ring or a bond. What I am pointing out is that this bill requires a fisherman to have something which he does not need to have to carry on his calling, whereas you require the farmer to have the very thing which it is necessary for him to have to be a farmer at all. The minister may be right that it is necessary to provide some test, but the test should not be that a fisherman should have a house and lot before 'he can borrow money in order to buy a boat. I think the thing to be done if this scheme is to be undertaken at all is to provide for security being taken on the gear or on the boat which is being bought, with a certain provision for depreciation and the country running a certain amount of risk. I do not think this bill will assist very much although I want to see it get off to the very best possible start.
May I .point out that I think there is entirely too much machinery in this act, with the number of inspectors and other people who have to inspect these properties and go over the credit situation when the most that can be loaned is one thousand dollars. It seems to me that we have cluttered it up a good deal by trying to adapt it to the farm loan act.

I understand that this vote is to assist the cheese industry and to prevent too great a proportion of the milk produced in the country being manufactured into butter and thus putting us on an export basis. Am I correct in stating that the minister has decided to bonus the production of cheese?
In great part, yes.
How will this bonus be paid and how much per pound will be paid?

It will be paid through the cheese factories directly to the farmers who take their milk to the factories. The first payment will be for July and will be on a basis of one and a quarter cents per pound. That is what is contemplated at the present time; it will be at least that. We shall be influenced to a certain extent, as to whether it will be a cent and a quarter or a cent and a half, by the latest reports for June with reference to the continued decrease in the production of cheese and increase in the production of butter, but it will be at least one cent and a quarter.
Through what medium will the producer be paid, and what proof will he be required to give that the cheese has been manufactured1 from his milk?

The cheese factory will have that record and they will have to give an affidavit to that effect. At the same time the cheese inspectors of the Department of Agriculture inspect well over ninety per cent of all cheese manufactured, and that also will be a check on the accuracy of the statement submitted by the -cheese factory itself.	_
I understand that the bonus in connection with the production of milk will start from the first of July, 1935.
That is the intention.
What is the estimated production of cheese for the present month, July, in connection with which the bonus will be paid?

The decrease in the production of cheese up to June 15 has been eighteen per cent as compared with a year ago. If that should continue, my information is that the quantity manufactured in the

On, the entire production of cheese for the rest of the year from the first of July up to the first of January- because cheese is produced somewhere in Canada up to that date-the government contemplates giving a direct bonus of from 1| cents to li cents to the cheese producer in Canada on the strength of vouchers produced by the several cheese factories, which bonus will be returned to the various producers through this medium.
Will this bonus apply to all the producers of cheese in Canada or only to those who come in under the marketing act?
It will apply to all producers in all the provinces-that is, to cheese in cheese factories.

Perhaps the minister did not hear my question. It is contemplated that from H cents to li cents will be paid on every pound of cheese manufactured from the first of July to the end of the year. Is that right?

It is contemplated that farmers sending milk to cheese factories will receive for the month of July and for each month thereafter in this year a bonus of at least li cents a pound on the cheese manufactured from their milk. It may be found necessary to increase it from li cents in order to divert a greater flow during the months when the volume will be greatest, but it is hoped not.

Is it anticipated that funds for the purpose of this bonus will be derived from other sources than this vote of $1,000,000? In other words, is it the intention to tax fluid milk in different milk sheds in order that the cheese producer may be bonused, or will a government bonus be adhered to entirely?
There is no thought of any levy being made on other farmers supplying whole milk to their markets in the cities or on any other farmer in the dairy industry.

Is it not true that a year ago it was necessary for the manufacturers of butter, through an arrangement, a mutual arrangement I believe, to dump some millions of pounds of surplus butter on the export market at less than the internal price?
Part of it was exported at a loss and part at a profit.

Suppose we once again find ourselves in that position in connection with butter which has to be dumped on the export market and sold there at less than the internal price. I understand that this cheese bonus applies to all cheese, whether consumed internally or exported. WTiat would be the policy of the government to meet a situation which undoubtedly will arise in connection with surplus butter for export? Is it intended to apply the bonus to the butter producer or only to the producer of cheese?
The purpose is to prevent that contingency arising. If it does arise it w'ill have to be considered on its merits.

There are other branches of agriculture and horticulture as well that are suffering. The fruit growers in my riding, indeed in the province of Ontario, not only lost an annual crop but in the winter of 1933-34 they lost their entire orchards after twenty-five years of planting and careful attention. These fruit growers have been absolutely wiped out; they lost their orchards. They are not in a position to produce any apples and it will take a lifetime or the better part of a lifetime to reproduce these orchards. I am strongly of the opinion that if we are to come to the assistance of the manufacturers of cheese, and if we are to do so with public funds, the fruit growers of Ontario have a justifiable case to present to the Department of Agriculture, and to submit a plan whereby the government should pay them so much a tree for every tree lost or frozen out, in view of the fact that their livelihood has been wiped out. Is there any reason why these fruit growers should not, under the precedent, ask for a bonus year by year until they can reproduce their orchards?
That is not a matter of marketing.

On general principles I am
opposed to bonusing. I rise now just to ask the minister why cheese in particular is singled out for payment of bonus out of the general taxes of this country. I do not see where we are going to stop. If it is proper to bonus the cheese producers, why is it not just as proper to bonus the producers of any other product of this country whether it is a natural product or not. Man does not live by bread alone. It is just as necessary for the producers to make a living out of producing

manufacturers are being and have been bonused for a number of years-

^ Resolved, that a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours that this house disagrees with their amendments to Bill No. 99, an act respecting radio broadcasting, for the following reasons:-
(1)	Bill 99 purported to amend The Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932, only to the extent that chapter 35 of the statutes of 1932-33, an act to amend The Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932, assented to on the 23rd May, 1932, should continue in force until the 31st March, 1936.
(2)	The amendments proposed by the Senate would have the effect of limiting the duration of the life of The Canadian Radio Broadcatsing Act, 1932, to the 31st March, 1936.
(3)	It is desirable that Bill No. 99 should be redrafted or amended so as to provide that The Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932, should remain in force indefinitely, but that the amendments made by chapter 35 of the statutes 1932-33 to such act should continue in force until the 31st March. 1936.
And this house respectfully suggests that the Senate should take the appropriate action to that end.
And that the clerk of the house do carry the said message to the Senate.
He said: Mr. Speaker, after discussion with the law officers it was found that there was a question as to whether or not the proposed amendment that left this house was inoperative to accomplish the end sought for the reason that it did not, in sufficiently clear terms, indicate that the purpose was to maintain in operation until March 31, 1936, the amendments adopted in 1932. The Senate, misconceiving for the moment the purposes that we had in mind, adopted as an amendment a provision that would have terminated the life of the main act, passed in 1932, on the 31st March, 1936. After having had the matter carefully looked into by the law officers it is believed that this motion will enable the Senate to adopt an amendment in accordance with the terms of the bill introduced here as Bill No. 99, which will remove any doubts as to the effectiveness of the legislation to accomplish the end proposed.

Natural Products Marketing Act-further amount required, $1,000,000.

I listened with a great deal of attention to the discussion of this item last night and this morning, and I feel that I must say a word in order to register my protest against this vote. The minister has been very industrious; he has striven very hard to show why the government were proposing this item, but in my opinion he has completely failed to indicate why there should be a premium for cheese rather than for sausages, potatoes or any other farm product. There is one reason, however, that he has not advanced, and the more I followed the discussion the more convinced I became that it was the real reason for this item. It is that the government feels very uneasy on the eve of an election as to the attitude it will take concerning the price of butter. I do not wish to deal with tiresome subjects, but it is known to very hon. member that in 1930 the question as to the price of butter was a very dominant factor in the victory of the Conservative party of that day. In those sections of my province in which I travelled it was in my opinion practically the only reason for the election of Conservative candidates. The
city population resisted very well the appeals made to it on labour and unemployment questions, at a time when unemployment was less serious than it is to-day. But in the rural parts of Quebec the butter question was the predominant one and appeals made by hon. members opposite indicating that if elected they would raise the price of butter were in my opinion the main reasons why the Liberal party lost many seats in that part of the country. I believe the same observations would apply to other parts of Canada.
I do not wish to turn from the item before us. May I observe that the government having failed to indicate why it would .place a premium upon cheese and not upon other products indicates that it wishes to have some argument to present to the farming population and to make its position easier due to the fact that instead of rising, as was promised in 1930. the price of butter has declined about ten cents per pound. That condition has obtained for the last four or five years.
The Minister of Agriculture has said that this vote offers the farming community an opportunity to make use of their .milk. It is a curious attitude to take, and we are surprised to find the minister telling the farming population, "We promised we would raise the price of your butter; we have failed to do that, the price having been reduced one-third of the 1930 price, an amount of ten cents, but we are going to do something else. We will help you not to produce butter and will make provision whereby you may use milk for other purposes." For these reasons it is proposed to spend $1,000,000 to induce the farming population to use surplus milk in the manufacture of cheese. As was well said yesterday by an hon. member from Ontario on this side of the house, such action would mean that the Canadian taxpayer will have to pay part of the price of the cheese we sell on the British and other markets. I say that is a wrong policy. Not only is it wrong in practice, and would lack effectiveness, but it is wrong in its inspiration.
If hon. members would look through the supplementary estimates they would find many millions of dollars provided for no purpose other than that of putting into practice reforms suggested by this government, not for the sake of reform but for the sake of having a political program to offer the Canadian electorate. Here is a million dollars which is not spent for cheese-unless we say that the retention of power is in itself a form of cheese. This session of parliament, with its very pretentious program of reform will cost

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
from $10,000,000 to $15,000,000 not to help the farmers, not to help this or that class but, in plain words, to make it easier for the government to face the electors or at least to alleviate the defeat in store for them.
I have discussed this matter; although I am not a rural member, especially in the last few months I have been travelling, and I have learned that the farmers do not expect very much from expenditures such as this one. But they will help the Conservative candidates in Missisquoi and Compton, and in other places where promises were made to the dairymen. Those candidates will be able to say, "Well, we have not been able to help you in securing a good price for butter; world conditions have been responsible. But we are doing the next best thing: We are taking money from the pockets of the taxpayers to pay towards the cheese which you will produce." That is a very bad policy. As a matter of fact, in a general way I will say that all these artificial reforms are bad. There is only one way tc help the community at large and that is to work towards a normal return to business conditions. But if you have to spend a million dollars to help one industry and another million dollars to help another part of the same industry you are simply replacing one evil by another and getting nowhere by way of social reform or improvement.
I shall not speak much longer, but after listening carefully to the explanation of the minister I must say he has not given a single reason why the money should be spent for cheese any more than for potatoes, sausages or anything else. Before sitting down I should like to make this suggestion. I suggest that he spend only $500,000 for cheese, and when the market becomes flooded with cheese he will have an other $500,000 to help the farmers in another direction. We would have to go on like that forever. As soon as he has overproduced one commodity he will have to spend another sum of money to improve another branch of the industry. I say that policy is all wrong. We should have good tariff conditions and good government, and I do not believe these millions of dollars being spent to enable the government to deceive the people by a program of reform which taken all in all, will never have any very good effect, will relieve the situation.
I believe the government is spending money in a very irresponsible manner and I must protest against it.

Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) has told the committee he does not like artificial methods, and among those methods he includes the stabilization scheme in aid of the dairy industry now before the committee. As to the general proposition I do not take exception to his expression of opinion, but I believe the hon. member will admit that the whole woild is in a state of dislocation. There come times in the health of the individual as in that of a nation, when it is necessary that he have recourse to extraordinary means. Stimulants in times of crises are admitted by all to be not o-nly wise but necessary. The hon. gentleman has not denied that it has been necessary to expend large sums of money in the city over whose municipal government he presided with great dignity for a period of two years. Some time back it would have been a source of astonishment to the hon. member had he known that it would be necessarjr to vote millions of dollars to provide for the sustenance of thousands of people in the prosperous city of Montreal. That is not the lot of Montreal alone but the lot of every large agglomeration of population throughout the civilized world. If it has been necessary to apply artificial means of sustenance to the urban population; why not to the rural? We know what has been done in England; we know what is being done in the United States. It has been necessary to resort during a period of disequilibrium to extraordinary methods. I have no particular desire, Mr. Chairman, to be drawn into a political controversy on this question. My hon. friend knows well that there has been set up in his province and in mine a dairy commission. He knows that the government of that province has fixed a definite price for milk, and he knows that, having fixed the price, that government has also fixed the quantity that may be sold at that price and has made no provision for the balance that is thrown back into the pot to be disposed of as best it may. These extraordinary measures were to meet extraordinary circumstances. We are confronted with many forces

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
flowing from disequilibrium. To meet them the country has paid large sums on account of unemployment. Suggestions are made to the house embracing reforestation, the building of highways, housing and other works which are not immediately necessary, to help those temporarily embarrassed. Should we not in fairness to ourselves and to the nation consider whether the proposal now engaging the attention of the committee is not worthy of approval?
I shall not waste much time on those lighthearted gentlemen who tell us that butter was worth so much five years ago or that our national revenue was so much five years ago. Every gentleman who is familiar with even the rudiments of economics and current affairs-
You did not say that in 1930.

My hon. friend knows
very well that the volume of trade between Great Britain and France which in the year 1930 was 1,300 billion francs shrivelled to less than 400. He knows that as well as all hon. gentlemen. So I am not going to waste much time in discussing what everybody who wishes to be serious already appreciates and is willing to admit.
Some reference has been made to promises about butter. My sins of omission and commission may be many, but I made no siuch promises. It is true that butter sold at a much higher price in 1930 than it is selling at now, but a point which I think hon. gentlemen should not overlook is that whereas in 1930 butter was selling at the world price, plus one cent duty-there was a spread of about one cent and a fraction-the spread under the present administration has been vastly increased until for the year 1934 the average price of butter in Canada was 22-29 cents, whereas in London, where the world price is fixed, it was but 15-65 cents. I draw this in all fairness to the attention of hon.. gentlemen opposite. The price of butter has gone down but there is a substantial increase in the price of Canadian butter compared with the world price of the same commodity. I do not mention these facts to score off anybody. But I am anxious to bring home to the people who wish to deal with this matter seriously an all important fact.
Now let us consider for one moment something that has been brought up not infrequently during the debate. Something has been said about tariffs; something has been said about manufacturers. Is it not a fact that the manufacturers, the industralists. the professional men, are all organized and organized for their own benefit? I do not say that they are organized for their own benefit exclusively but they are organized so that their affairs may be conducted in an orderly way. In my own profession, for instance, rules have been enacted for its government. There are rules which discipline members of the bar and there are means of exacting a certain level of conduct from each of them. There are other rules which apply to emoluments. That is true also of the medical profession; it is true of organized labour, whether it be railway labour, the iron workers or the garment workers. Wherever we go in professional and industrial life we find organization and a measure of discipline and a measure of control. Broadly speaking it is true that the only element of our population which is not organized, the only element which is at the mercy of wind and wave, of greed and exploitation, is the primary producer. Never has the primary producer of this country been willing to yield u,p enough of his individuality and his so-called liberty to reap the benefits of discipline and order. I believe that this government has enacted a measure, the marketing act, which affords to the primary producer the opportunity to give himself a labour union, the opportunity to give himself a professional organization, that from it may flow discipline and the benefits which come from order and hierarchy. I submit this to the committee; if the farmers organize under this act, as already groups have done-we have been given details with respect to the producers of different commodities, apples, potatoes, chickens; the milk producers in British Columbia, who have all sought the shelter of the marketing act and are satisfied with it-if the dairymen of this country will organize, and it is a vast undertaking because this industry is represented in every province and in every section of every province in the dominion, it seems to me they will benefit and that we should afford to them while in process of organization a measure of. succour and support. They require assistance, they require encouragement, until equilibrium is reestablished.
So long as my memory runs,, the farmers in the southeastern counties of Quebec have shipped their dairy produce in the form of sweet cream and fresh milk to the industrial centres of New England. Without a moment's warning a dyke-the Hawl'ey-Smoot tariff-was raised which dammed back that generous stream until it flooded out the farmers living in that locality. TV hile we had that ready market it was possible for

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
us to import butter from Australia aind New Zealand1 to good advantage, but when that market was taken away it was necessary that something be done for these farmers. While some hon. gentlemen regret that tariffs in this country are so high, most hon. members -I make one exception and bow low to the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young)- admit that evil though they may be, they are a necessary evil. We have had to enact tariffs to preserve the life of our industry and the standard' of living of our industrial workers. If that is a sound argument for industry, I submit that we should do something to protect this vast section of the community which is not protected. I submit further that while these changes are being brought about it is doing scant justice and providing rather skimpy generosity to vote a million dollars for the stabilization of the greatest industry in Canada.
I do not see how any hon. gentleman who is even remotely familiar with the dairy industry can question the wisdom of exporting our surplus in a form fhat commands a premium in the worlds market. At the present time our cheese-I admit that there are certain accidents as to age and scarcity tending to raise the price-brings four cents per pound more in Great Britain than the cheese of our rivals for that market. Hon. gentlemen opposite have stated that out butter is of an inferior quality and does not bring as good a price in the world maiket as does the commodity produced by our competitors.	If that be true, and I do not
think it is questioned, is it not in the interests of the dairymen-dairying is the principal part, wheat notwithstanding, of Canadian agriculture-to make at least an effort during a moment of .trial to stabilize prices and to bring about some measure of relief? I think it was the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraseir)) who asked if a small amount like $1,000,000 would be adequate for the stabilization of this vast industry. That is a fair question, the answer is that only a small fraction of the total production of butter goes into the export market and it is that- small fraction which raises havoc with prices. ' Our price here is the price of our demand plus our protection until we have a surplus and then we must take the price that is offered to us in the markets of the world.
\\ e have come to the assistance of different elements in the country. We have voted millions in aid of industrial' employment; we have voted other millions for this and that activity, but because this vast farming industry happens to be unorganized it has been 
forgotten in the past. It seems to me that there is a promise of brighter days for the farmer if he will avail himself of the possibilities of the marketing act and is given some encouragement and stimulus while efforts are being made to bring him under that act.

Does the hon. member not remember that we shut out imports of butter from Australia because it was being exported to this country under a plan similar to that proposed and supported by the government?
No.
Oh yes, the Patterson plan.

As I recall the Patterson plan,, it was one under which the producers of butter contributed to a fund a certain amount per pound produced and a certain amount per pound was taken from that fund and applied to each pound1 exported. Even were I to grant the premise of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore), which unfortunately I cannot, the situation is entirely different. The scheme which is outlined here is one by which assistance is given to the producer whether or not his product finds its way into a foreign market.

I have no desire to be supercritical of this vote and I do not intend to criticize it until I find out how it is related to the marketing act. It is usual for a marketing scheme to be set up before you pass a vote of this kind. I happened to be in Leeds and Lanark counties during the week-end and I discussed this matter with a number of farmers, but they did not seem to understand it at all any more than I did. They told me that they had asked for a bonus of two cents per pound on all cheese exported, and I suppose this vote is the answer. After reading this designated vote one could easily conclude that it was for organization purposes under the Marketing Act rather than for a subsidy to cheese. Would the minister give an anxious inquirer the connection between this vote and the marketing act? I think every hon. member is sympathetic towards the dairying industry, as that industry is so closely allied to the health of the people and the fertility of the soil. This industry means practically to the east what the wheat industry means to the prairies and it deserves our close and sympathetic attention. I have no doubt that if provision were made for a straight subsidy of one and one half cents

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
per pound on all exported cheese the minister would not be able to find an objector, but it is a different thing when this matter is brought in in this furtive and mysterious way. I am really in a dilemma and I wish the minister would disentangle me. .

It is intended that a great part of this vote will be expended under the provisions of section 9 of the Natural Products Marketing Act, but a scheme would not be set up, as the hon. member will appreciate, until the money is made available. When the money is made available it is intended to set up a scheme to equalize the dairy industry and provide assistance to those farmers who send their milk to the cheese factories.

I rather suspected that was the situation although I did not know. Section 9 was one of the most objectionable sections of this bill so far as the *opposition were concerned, and instead of making the bill more acceptable to us the minister is endeavouring to make it more objectionable. And the same remark may be made with regard to the amendments he brought down; two of them were very objectionable. Now we have him invoking section 9 without the farmers having taken any initiative whatever. Under section 9 the minister has authority, if he considers that any product is prejudicially affected under the marketing conditions that surround us, to take the initiative himself and work through any local board ior agency he desires, and he instructs the central board to proceed as if it had been asked for. What is the matter with the Ontario dairymen that they cannot ask for something which on the face of it is so good? Why should the minister have to come to the rescue and ask for it on their behalf? That is the point I am concerned about. If he will bring down a straight subsidy to the dairy industry, especially the cheese industry, there will not be much comment upon it; but I cannot understand why he should proceed in this mysterious way on his own initiative in one of the oldest districts of Ontario. Why cannot the dairy industry in this province take the initiative instead of the minister doing so?

Last week the minister introduced and passed through this house a bill amending the marketing act, which provided that a fund be set up to be raised by a levy on the commodity concerned, and the explanation he gave of the use to be made of
the fund was identically the same as the use to which this million dollars will be put. Is this million dollars a substitute for the fund he proposes to raise by that levy, or is it in addition thereto?

It is in addition thereto, not a substitute. The bill to which the hon. gentleman refers was not introduced for the purpose of setting up a fund. When I was asked as to what use might be made of the section, I said it might be used in this way.

Then there will be more than one million dollars available for the purpose. In addition to the million voted by the taxpayers, all those engaged in the dairy industry will be subject to a tax which they will have to pay or go to gaol.
No; the hon. member is confusing matters. There is no levy, there is no tax of any kind associated with this million.

Then I must ask the minister to explain again the bill he brought in the other night, because when we asked for an example of the way in which the money would be spent he used the very illustration of butter and cheese and said that the money so levied would be used to bonus the farmers to stay in the production of cheese and not to go into butter.
If they submitted a scheme to do it that way.

I remember distinctly that the explanation the minister gave was as the hon. member for Weyburn has stated, and I expressed my lack of understanding of the whole intent of that bill. That was why I thought that this vote of one million dollars was for an entirely different purpose. I hope the minister will help me out in my understanding of it now. How is it that the Ontario dairymen do not take the initiative themselves in setting up a marketing scheme, instead of the minister stepping in himself and doing it for them. Can they not take on a good thing when they see it without waiting for the minister to do the taking on>, just before an election, though that is incidental? I do not mind that; you can pack this chamber full of bills and votes of this kind and it will not save these hon. gentlemen from their impending doom, so that that does not concern me. Selfpreservation is the first law of nature and we concede them the right to hang on to every straw they can get their claws on

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
between now and election time. But I do not want to be put in the position of an unfriendly critic of this million if it is going to the dairy industry and they want it through a marketing scheme. They cannot want it very ardently or they would have organized themselves under the marketing act. They want two cents per pound straight bonus on their cheese as far as I can make out, and here under an item entitled Natural Products Marketing Act we have $1,000,000. No wonder no one understands what it is for.

I regret from what was said the other night, that hon. members should have gathered the impression that this million was to be used in addition to or in conjunction with any levy made, because I am quite certain that I did not say so, and if they will read my remarks they will see that I did not say anything that would convey that impression. The hon. gentleman asks why the dairy farmers of Ontario have not submitted some scheme under tile marketing act. They have, in conjunction with the dairy farmers of every other province in the dominion. But, as I 'have stated, the difficulty of organizing an industry in which so many people take part, hundreds of thousands of farmers, is such that it cannot be done in a very short period. Hon. gentlemen would seem to give the impression that little advantage has been taken of the marketing act to date, and the- thing I have always kept in mind, especially while in committee in the house, ife the great contrast- between the opposition advanced against the measure when it was introduced and what has actually been taking place among the great farming population of Canada, who have been taking advantage of it. The board was set up only inAugust, and already there is under the administration of the marketing act, and taking advantage of its provisions, over $43,000,000 worth of annual business. Not only that, but there are applications from farmers to have provision made to enable them to make use of the act to be extent of a further S240.000.000. In other words, the producers of $280,000,000 odd of produce have applied to come under the administration of the act without any effort on the part of the dominion government or of the marketing board to lead people to take advantage of its provisions. It is simply the natural outcome of what has been taking place, and the thoughts that have been in the minds of farmers throughout the country for years. We had men who devoted the greater part of their lives, without thought of reward of any kind, to the development of a cooperative marketing system among the 
farmers so that they would by voluntary effort be able to rid themselves of what they regarded als a great deal of unnecessary waste and cost in getting their products to market. Every hon. member who is a farmer must have in mind the names of some of these men. We had Mr. Morrison of Ontario, Mr. Wood of Alberta, Mr. McPhail of Saskatchewan and many others, whose great regret was that, although they realized that they had accomplished a great deal in- the way of voluntary cooperation, the forces for which they had laboured so long and unselfishly were still unorganized to such an extent as to leave themlselves a ready prey to those who were more concerned with their own selfish interests and Who were ready to take advantage of the unorganized farming community. The fact that that work had been done and that the farmers were anxious that a further step should be taken is evidenced by the number of applications that have come in-applications to the extent of $280,000,000 of agricultural business apart from wheat.
I was the first to state in this house, when I moved the resolution leading to this act, that there would be many obstacles which we could not foresee. No one could expect otherwise in a change in the marketing of the products of the farm, and which was to take the place of a system that had been built up but was regarded by the farmers as not giving that service which it should. Therefore I maintain that it is a great and undoubted proof of the feeling on the part of a great body of farmers in this country that in this short period, especially in view of the misrepresentations by great sections of the press and also by hon. members opposite as to the benefit that can be derived from the Natural Products Marketing Act, these farmers have availed themselves to this extent and expressed themselves as being strongly in favour of it. I am not talking of men of academic minds as has been suggested here, but as I am making this statement I have in mind men not even friendly to the old pool organizations, wheat, live stock or otherwise, but men who through their own individual effort, rugged individualists as some hon. members might prefer to call them, have made a great success of farming even against the obstacle of poor markets. These men have offered the best they have and have given freely of their time during the past months, especially in the winter season, to see if they could formulate some scheme. They have finally agreed in the three western provinces, where they have the greatest proportion of live stock in this country, upon a

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
scheme that they believe will be of use in the marketing of their products. These men are actual farmers, men who own and control up to five or six thousand head of cattle. One sheep rancher in British Columbia who at first was opposed to the marketing act because of the .misrepresentations he saw in the press and heard from the platform, is now one hundred per cent behind it. This year his marketing of lambs and ewes will be up to 6,000 head.
When I stand here-and I have sat here through weeks of hostility because it cannot be described as anything else-the thing that is foremost in my mind is this great movement among the farmers that cannot be denied, that cannot be stopped, because what the farmer wants more than .anything else is a greater pride in his occupation, and the only way in which he will get that is by having more power in the administration of his own business. Nothing will stop him from getting this. What has been the opposition to this measure? The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) for weeks opposed it and his opposition has been proved to be unwarranted. One of the points on which he laid the greatest emphasis was that there would be a restriction of production. There has been none. Another point he raised was that there was a great fear in his heart that the farmers, if they united and organized themselves, would injure other bodies in the community. They have not shown any evidence of attempting to do that; all they want is to be let alone, to progress quietly, to go forward and organize themselves, so that they may be able to market their products to better advantage.
Then we had the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott), the former Minister of Public Works, and I remember reading an account of some of his speeches early last fall when he ridiculed the number of licences that would have to be issued to license producers from one end of the country to the other, a statement which was very far wide of the mark.

I was just quoting the
minister's statement as to the number that might be issued. It is on Hansard.

When the measure
was in its final stages, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) said that it was only a political measure; that it would never be put into effect, yet it was put into effect a month after he made the statement. The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) at a meeting at Wingham-and I happened to be there that day although I
was a little late to attend the meeting-made the statement that the act would never be put into effect although he must have known that it was in effect at the time he made the statement.
Yet in opposition to this great movement among the agriculturists of this country to take advantage of the act to make it possible for them to organize in their own interest, a right which has been given to other bodies in the dominion before, what have we had? Lawyers, chiefly from the cities; people who profess to be farmers and who to a certain extent are farmers but whose chief business is not farming but something other than farming. How many simon pure, bona fide farmers in the House of Commons, whose chief interest is farming, have opposed this measure? Few. The opposition against this great demand or cry on the part of the farmers themselves for this to be made available to them has come chiefly from lawyers from the cities by twisting a word here and a word there especially when they think this will be to their political advantage.
