I have endeavoured to make it clear in the past that the question whether the individual shall receive a loan must depend entirely on the merits and circumstances of each individual case. There are no employees of either department working on commission, and if my hon. friend will give me in confidence the names of the individuals I will inquire by wire immediately to see what activity is taking place there, because the course he suggests is entirely foreign to the proper authorization of either act.

I thank the minister for his explanation, because I know of several men who are so working. The Conservative organizer in the last provincial election has been going throughout my constituency and I did not know whether this was his occupation or whether he was doing it for political purposes.
Is the official receiver under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act the representative of the farm loan board under the Farm Loan Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; he has no official contact at all.

In Ontario, at least in1 the western part, the official receiver is the gentleman who is handling the forms. I cannot say that he is doing as much as the men to whom my hon. friend from Willow Bunch has referred, but certainly he is giving the farmers to understand that they must come to him if they want loans; and as recently as last week I obtained some forms from the official receiver, who stated then that he was the representative of the farm loan board in that district.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There can be no objection to the farm loan board, as a matter of convenience, asking another employee, of the government, the official receiver for instance, to keep in his possession and make available to farmers the necessary forms. I can see no objection to that.
I do not abject; I asked whether that was being done and the minister replied no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was not as far as I know, but I am .prepared to accept the hon. gentleman's statement. But I have no hesitation in saying ,-jhat no one, neither the official receiver nor anyone else, has the right to tell a farmer that he can secure a loan as a matter of right.
Is this representative of the Finance department a permanent official?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is a permanent official appointed in virtue of an amendment to the act passed this year.
Does not the minister think it is proper to have his name put in while he is given an allowance over and above his salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would be, except for two reasons. The Farm Loan Act as amended provides for alternative officials so that it does not follow of necessity that the same official
Supply-Miscellaneous

will continue in the office. The other reason is this. I prefer not to put his name here at all because, he is receiving a salary out of proportion to the services rendered and this is a matter of justice to this official.
How many persons have made compositions under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and received loans under the Canadian Farm Loan Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have none of that information here but I will make inquiries and endeavour if possible to get it.

Item agreed to.
The Economic Council of Canada Act, 1935,
Has the economic council been appointed, and if so, who are the members?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The members of the council have not yet been named.

This is a revelation. It was so necessary to have this economic council, this crutch was so necessary for the Prime Minister that he could not get along without it, and yet we have all the social legislation passed without the assistance of the council- most ridiculous, most absurd. If it was so necessary why did they wait so long to appoint the members of the council-and they have not yet appointed them. In their wisdom they have got along without the council; why do they not do the same in the future? All the reform program has been implemented with the exception of one or two matters. This is superfluous; it is pure extravagance, just as ridiculous as the stovepipe letter boxes and all official expenditures made in the same quarter. I hope this vote will be dropped; I will not stand for it at all. I say, it^is most ridiculous. What do we need a brain trust for if it has not yet been in action? Twenty thousand dollars is something; a family could live a long time on that sum. This is another red tape official expenditure.

Item agreed to.
To provide hereby, notwithstanding anything contained in The Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act or any other act or law, for payment out of the consolidated revenue fund' to the present Canadian minister to France of an annuity at the rate of $3,000. to commence upon his retirement and to continue thereafter at the above rate during his lifetime, $3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that the occasion for passing this appropriation has not arisen, and I therefore move that item 414 be reduced in the sum of $3,000.
Does the minister mean that there is no intention of making a retirement such as is indicated in this item?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The present incumbent
of the position in question was appointed in May, 1911. A change of government took place in September of that year and he was continued in office. He was appointed a minister and he has now reached the age of sixty-seven. The British practice is that ministers retire at sixty. This provision was put into the estimates in order to provide for that contingency. The impaired hearing of the minister makes it impossible for him to function properly and unfortunately that has been the case for some time, but he has not resigned his post and this item is therefore superfluous.

Do I understand that
it is not the intention to recall the minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have nothing to say as to that.

Then I shall have to
say a word or two about the matter. This position in Paris is of course different from the others to this extent, that when the present incumbent was appointed, it was merely a commissariat; he was made a commissioner for Canada in France succeeding the late Mr. Fabre who had been there for a very great number of years. Mr. Fabre was the first appointee there and he was kept as representative of Canada until he died. Mr. Roy was appointed-and at the time I was a member of parliament-after the Laurier government then in office found difficulty in getting somebody because the position was not very attractive at that time and meant the absence of the appointee and his family from Canada and their settlement in France. In 1927 or 1928 the office was changed into a legation and he became the first plenipotentiary and minister for Canada in France. Mr. Roy has been there for the past twenty-five years rendering great sendee to Canada. I desire to read an editorial in the Montreal Star of Thursday, June 27. The writer was obviously under the impression that Mr. Roy was retiring, as I now understand he is not. This is the editorial which reads:
A Good and Faithful Servant
Hon. Philippe Roy, Canadian Minister to France, has without doubt richly earned the leisure and repose which his impending retirement, just announced, will bring to him. But there will be general regret, both in Canada and in France, that the term of his long service is drawing to a close.

Supply-Minister to France
To those whose memories carry back to an earlier day, the work which Mr. Roy has done for Canada in France is especially clear. The Canadian commissioner's office, before his day, was a small upstairs affair on a street little known to strangers in Paris, with an almost non-existent staff, with facilities so restricted as to cripple any work it might have hoped to do, either for Canadians abroad or for Canadian business. Mr. Roy changed all that. He moved the Canadian office to the Grand boulevard; he made it a comfortable and spacious place where the "Canadian errant" was made welcome and happy; he "put Canada on the map" of boulevardier consciousness; he was personally the soul of generosity and hospitality and, withal, a shrewd and able business man with Canadian interests always before his mind. How much of the betterment of Franco-Canadian trade was due to Mr. Roy's acumen and to his thorough knowledge of the opportunities for increased business between the two countries, it is, of course, impossible to estimate definitely, but there is no question that his services in this respect have been exceedingly valuable. The splendid Cite Universitaire project was very largely his plan, a contribution to an intellectual and cultural bond between Canada and France that cannot be estimated from blue books or trade returns. Mr. Roy has deserved well of Canada and the thanks of both French-and English 

speaking Canadians are due to him.
May I recall his services during the war? Mt. Roy was like a father to ail Canadian soldiers. His place, not only his office but his residence, was open to all members of the Canadian forces, and they all knew that as well as I do. He has always enjoyed not only the respect but the esteem and confidence of every public man in France in all spheres of national activity ovier there, and to think under the circumstances of retiring him compulsorily with a pension of $3,000 when one considers what is being paid by way of superannuation to judges or military men, is humiliating. However, he is not so old; he is only-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Sixty-seven, two years
older than I am.

He is two years older
than the Prime Minister, but I am sure my right hon. friend in two years will still be able to fulfil his duties whatever they may be at that time.
Mr. DURAiNLEAU:	They will be the
same.

I know Mr. Roy very
well; I have always been an intimate friend of his and I know he is still able to fulfil his function, to do his work. His hearing is better now than it was a couple of years ago. I know the government can recall him; a plenipotentiary minister is subject to recall. He has to be persona grata not only to the
government that receives him but also of course to the government that sends him to the foreign country. But under the circumstances, especially at this time when the government is at the end of its term of office, just before a general election which may bring into power another government, to send to France a. minister representative of that future government does not seem the fair thing to do. Of course nobody knows the future, but if I have a share of influence in the future government of Canada, the man who under such circumstances would go there to replace Mr. Roy would be well advised to buy a round-trip ticket.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With much that the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) has said I am heartily in accord. It must have occurred to him that considerations such as those to which he has referred were in the mind of the government of the day, for Mr. Roy has remained' in office since August, 1930, notwithstanding the fact that I have believed that at times his physical condition was not such, because of his poor hearing, as would enable him to function as he should like, he has remained there because, as the hon. gentleman has said, he has discharged difficult tasks with success.
I do not think anyone will quarrel with what the hon. gentleman has said, but I can only say that the difficulty has been the question of a pension. In Great Britain the rule is that career ministers and ambassadors retire at sixty. Some time ago we passed an order in council under which we retired those in the civil service who had reached the age of sixty-five. The banks and other institutions in this country adopted a regulation under which they retire their officials at sixty, because of the conditions referred to in the banking and commerce committee last year. No contribution is made by any minister to the superannuation fund, and any sum that is voted comes directly from the taxpayers. It is an extremely difficult thing to justify, and it was with great personal reluctance that this item was inserted in the estimates at all. Apparently I was wrongly informed with regard to the intentions of Mr. Roy; apparently he does not desire to leave his post, although he has attained the age of sixty-seven.
There must be some understanding with respect to all the ministers in the service of this country. My own view is that the English rule is satisfactory, and the provision for pensions in England would not entitle the present incumbent of the office at Paris to the sum here indicated, for he has been a minister for only a very limited time. It
Supply-Minister to France

is true that he served from 1911 to 1927-28 as high commissioner, but it was by his own choice that he went to Paris. He preferred that to remaining in Canada, which neeessi-tated leaving his practice in Edmonton for half the year and coming to the Senate. I think that is a well known fact which he himself has stated frequently. So far as the service is concerned it must be known to all members of this house that the only legation in which there was a vacancy when the government came into office, or where a vacancy has occurred since, was at Washington. Sir Herbert Marler, who was appointed to Tokyo by hon. gentlemen opposite, has remained there and no one has suggested that a change of government should result in a change of ministeis. I have not looked upon it in that way at all, but there must be times when the public service demands that those who hold office should surrender it.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the hon. gentleman
is always thinking of the spoils of office; he thinks of them so constantly that he cannot even forget them in his dealings with some of his fellow members. Need I .mention that Sir Herbert Marler was appointed by a Liberal administration, but he has continued in office and is discharging his duties to this administration as faithfully as he discharged them to the last administration. I do not look upon a minister as being in quite the position suggested by the hon. gentleman. Far be it from me to suggest that a minister would want to remain in office who found it impossible to function because of his attitude of mind towards the government he was serving, and as conditions are it is difficult to transfer ministers from one point to another; there are so few of them. As I said a moment ago, of necessity .there must be an age when men should retire from these posts. In Great Britain that age has been settled at sixty; in this country we have fixed that age as sixty-five, and while it is quite true that technically the civil service regulations do not apply to ministers and sixty-five is not an age for compulsory retirement while seventy is, in experience in the older countries it has been found that the age I have suggested is reasonable.
I know there is not a member of this house who does not realize that those who hold office under those circumstances should not be easily disturbed.. But if, as is the case in some of our courts in Canada, men, are unable to hear and have to use devices placed upon their desks to enable them to hear what is said, surely it cannot be said that this is 
a proper discharge of their judicial duties. I find it difficult, I confess, to understand how men continue to sit as judges and to draw the public money under those circumstances. I am not ignorant of the fact a few months ago, at the meeting of the Canadian Bar Association,, an eminent judge condemned both the hon. gentleman who has just spoken and this government for endeavours made to amend the Judges Act, and the condemnation against my hon. friend was greater because he succeeded and I did not.
My bill was better advised than the bill of my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend says his bill was better calculated to serve the immediate purpose than the bill we sponsored. I just put this to the committee: If a man holds himself out as an expert in any branch of human endeavour, and is so employed; if he ceases to be able to give that expert service for which he was employed, certainly he would find great difficulty in a court of law in recovering his salary, stipend or compensation. There is an implied undertaking on the part of those who occupy positions such as these that they are physically fit to discharge their duties. I realize that, for instance, with respect to the office which I hold. I think it must be perfectly clear that a prime minister, whoever he is, must be physically able to discharge his duties; if he is not he should retire. I think the same thing is true with respect to members of the judiciary and others. But in view of the erroneous impression which I had, and in view of the fact that Mr. Roy does not desire to retire, this item should disappear from the estimates. I should like my hon. friend to realize, however, that I regard this as an exceedingly generous provision for one who has held office as a minister for so short a time, and who has made no contribution to the superannuation fund. I could give cases so numerous as to weary the committee of efforts made to secure small pensions, or what might be regarded as adequate pensions, that have failed because of what I have just mentioned.
Now that we have an understanding of the situation I ask the Minister of Finance to withdraw the item from the estimates. I repeat, however, that I do think if the hon. gentleman will consider the matter carefully he will regard this as a much more generous provision than is usually made for those occupying positions similar to that occupied by the gentleman in question. I do not desire to detract in any sense from what my

Supply-Minister to France
hon. friend has said as to the services rendered by Mr. Roy in Paris. Apparently, however, I did have an entirely erroneous understanding with regard to his recognition of the limitations imposed upon him, by conditions over which he had no control, to further discharge his duties.

The Prime Minister has indicated that he is largely in accord with what the hon. member for Quebec East has said respecting the Hon. Philippe Roy who is at present the minister representing Canada in Paris. I should like to join my hon. friend and the right hon. gentleman in their observations, and to add that I believe it would be impossible to pay too generous a tribute to the services Mr. Roy has rendered Canada during the time he has held public positions in Paris. I do not believe it would be fair to estimate an allowance to which he might be entitled simply by a computation of the time he has been minister. As has been mentioned Mr. Roy has represented Canada in France since May, 1911. That is nearly a quarter of a century, and includes the trying and difficult period of the war. During the whole of that period and indeed ever since he resided in Canada Mr. Roy's home, as is well known, has been an open house to Canadians. Especially during the war, the services of both Mr. Roy and Madame Roy were placed at the disposition not only of this country but also of France in a manner which could not have been excelled.
It is known, too, that Mr. Roy has held an unique position in Paris both as regards what he has done for Canadians who have gone to that city on official missions or otherwise, and with respect to the confidence he has enjoyed with the members of whatever government may have been in office in France. I do not believe any minister, of any government, at any time, has Shared to a fuller degree the confidence of the government to which he has been accredited than has the Hon. Philippe Roy in Paris. I would say, too, that confidence has been enjoyed in equal measure by different British ambassadors who have been resident in Paris. As is known, our country along with other countries has membership in the league of nations, and the minister at Paris has exceptional knowledge of many of the matters which have come before and which pertain to that body. In fact, to some degree he has been the one Canadian minister dealing with European affairs. I do believe that when the time comes to arrange his retiring allowance the government having to do therewith should feel more than justified in considering the entire time
Mr. Roy has served in Paris in a representative capacity as being equal to that which it would have been had 'he been a minister from the beginning.
Inasmuch as the Prime Minister has referred to the subject I should like to sgy that I believe both he and I are in entire agreement as to the time having come when, with respect to the diplomatic service of Canada, there should be some act of parliament governing the service, which would set out specifically the constributions if any to be made by those who are members of the service, on what basis retirement may be effected, and in what amounts retirement allowances should be granted. If the government had seen fit to bring in a measure of that kind we might well have discussed it, and possibly could have agreed upon it, and have taken action under it. I believe, however, that a measure of the kind might more properly be brought in at the beginning of a new parliament rather than at the close of an 'old one. I mention the subject at this time, however, so that no matter what the complexion of the new parliament may be there may come from this House of Commons an expression indicating that we do believe- and I believe I may make this observation for hon. members in all sections of the chamber-that if we are to continue to have a diplomatic service the whole service should be regularized as to appointments thereto and retirements therefrom in a manner similar to that followed in the British and other diplomatic services.
I must confess to some degree of relief and satisfaction at what I understood the Prime Minister to say, namely, that there was no intention to retire Mr. Roy at this time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not mention that at all.

My right hon. friend did not mention it? Well, I am glad there is opportunity to avoid misunderstanding about it, because what I am about to say should I believe be said at this time. The diplomatic service is somewhat different from other branches of the public service. I have heard my right hon. friend say-he said it expressly in connection with the London appointment-that in making an appointment to that position no government should be expected necessarily to retain the appointee of a previous administration, and that there should at least be an opportunity to a new administration of making an appointment of some one who would be persona grata to itself. That I believe was a perfectly sound point of view.
Supply-Minister to France

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was limited to political appointments, and did not apply to diplomatic appointments.

May I say that what my right hon. friend is contending for may be perfectly sound where diplomatic appointments are made under civil service requirements and in accordance with civil service rules. But I believe the circumstances are entirely different where an appointment is being made to the diplomatic service, of any person who has not up to the time of such appointment been in the diplomatic sendee, and where such appointment is not in the nature of a promotion within that service.
May I be concrete in my observations and for the moment assume conditions which may or may not arise. In the event of the Liberal party being returned to office I for one would feel that it would mean very much to the government of the day to have the Hon. Philippe Roy in the position of minister at Paris, even if his services were to be retained there for only a short time. He is more familiar than any other person could possibly be with the many matters about which an administration would wish to have full knowledge. He is familiar, for example with all that up to the present has been done in connection with the negotiation of trade agreements. He is familiar, too, with the personnel of, and enjoys the confidence of, members of past and present French governments, and particularly of persons whom a new administration might wish to meet or consult. For these reasons ahd many others he would, for a new administration, fill the position more effectively than any other person could possibly fill it. Assuming that Mr. Roy is to be retired at some time, however soon or late, I submit that it should not be until after a new parliament has come into being. At that time whatever administration may be in office could indicate its wishes and have them carried out as might be considered necessary. I would certainly feel, however, that if between now and that time an appointment were made to the position of minister in Paris of a person who did not enjoy to the same degree the confidence of a new administration that Mr. Roy has enjoyed, no obligation should or would rest upon a new ministry to retain the services of such person.
I have thought it well to make these observations so that there may be no misunderstanding or possibility of hard feeling in connection with anything which may or may not take place. From what has been said this afternoon I hope it will be sufficiently clear that

Mr. Roy is continuing in office to meet whatever fate may come to him sooner or later, and that the decision, whether sooner or later, which is to determine that fate will not be made until the people have spoken and have indicated the administration they wish to have in office during the next few years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I must make one further observation. Frequently I have endeavoured to make it clear that in my judgment the position of high commissioner in London is entirely different from that of a diplomatic representative of Canada. One is surely a representative of the government and the other a representative of the Sovereign. The diplomatic representatives who serve us at Tokyo, Paris and other centres are not necessarily representatives of the government, in the narrow political sense. I have acted upon that. If the doctrine suggested had been acted upon we would have retired Sir Herbert Marler from Tokyo and Mr. Roy from Paris shortly after we took office. That has not been done. They have continued in their positions because they were representatives not of a government, but of the country and the King. So long as they continued to discharge their duties in a manner acceptable to the government their former political faith we believed should not be the governing factor in connection with their retention in office. We have acted upon that principle. I will admit that the right hon. gentleman opposite protbably would not have done it under similar circumstances.
My right hon. friend should not say that. It is not fair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In view of what he said. Here we had Sir Herbert Marler, a former member of his administration. Just think what that means. Here was a' former member of the Liberal administration appointed to Tokyo, and yet we have not asked him to retire. Here was a former Liberal senator, a well known and a very pronounced Liberal, very strong in his convictions and in the expression of his opinions, and yet no effort was made to retire him.
In the case of the high commissioner at London I think that the position can be put very simply. HS under statute is a political officer. The statute itself indicates that he is a representative of the government, and as I indicated, in the very nature of things he is more closely in touch with the government a^hd with their policies and views than any man who occupies a purely diplomatic post. He has under the statute to deal with so many

Supply-Minister to France
matters that it is quite clear that that is so. It is an old story now but we certainly did inform Mr. Massey that we thought he should retire from the post to which he had been appointed in the closing days of the former administration, and he did retire accordingly.
I think on second thought most men would realize that that was a sound position. I feel perfectly certain that the present high commissioner in London in the event of a change in government wull regard it as his duty to retire at once, and I feel equally certain that whether he did or not he would be retired.
I understood he had his passage taken already.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I know that the right
hon. gentleman has sources of information that I have not, but I have no such information as would lead1 me to any such conclusion. He usually comes to this country for his vacation, but he has not even yet applied for leave for his vacation. He usually takes it, if my memory serves me, in August or September, but as I say he has not even yet applied' for leave.
I make clear the distinction between the diplomatic position that a minister who serves his country occupies and1 the position of high commissioner. It never has been the case in England that a minister is retired because there has been a change of government, so far as I have been able to ascertain. If the minister is thought not to be the best available appointment for a particular position he is transferred to another post and somebody else takes his place. That is my information from inquiries.
There is just one thing I do want to say, and it is this:	It is not necessary to introduce a statute as the matter stands at present with respect to ministers. I suppose the right hon. gentleman did1 give some attention to it himself. The fact is that the regulations which are issued in Great Britain with respect to ministers and ambassadors are promulgated by order in council because they are the expression of the terms under which the sovereign's representative discharges his functions in foreign countries. I would put it this way. We had intended1 to promulgate such regulations and had prepared them accordingly, but in view of the fact that we had but three ministers and that we had passed the general regulations respecting our civil sendee we did not desire to seem to be endeavouring to press unduly, Shall I say. the views which we held as to the desirability of the general terms of the British regulations applying to our own country. The matter rests there.. If the minister does not
desire to relinquish his post under the circumstances to which I have alluded, that is a matter for him to consider. I do not think it is necessary to suggest that if anyone is appointed the practice which we have pursued would not be followed by hon. gentlemen apposite. We know their attitude of mind would not be quite ours with respect to that matter. We are perfectly certain that if we were to appoint anybody as minister he would be removed as quickly as possible.

I do not like to enter
[DOT]into a controversy with my right hon. friend as to the status of the ministers representing Canada in foreign countries. He states that those who are diplomatic agents are in a different position from the high commissioner, and seems to suggest that it is not necessary that they should represent their government to the same extent as the high commissioner. Well, the ministers, like the ambassadors, are appointed by a commission under the great seal. They are not ordinary public servants. They are envoys, they are plenipotentiaries, sent to represent their country in a foreign country, and they are subject to recall at any time. I took the trouble to say that my right hon. friend might have done it. They are ambassadors, they are plenipotentiaries, and the country .that sends them surely can recall them at any time. Their country is forced to recall them and to issue what is called letters of recall when the country to which they are accredited desires that they be recalled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is very seldom done. There has been only one case on the American continent.

So far as being forced
to recall them, that is very seldom done, but in the diplomatic service of any country which has a large number of ministers they are being recalled all t/he time. As a matter of fact, France since the opening of its legation here has had three ministers within seven years. Mr. Knight was recalled and was replace by Mr. Arsene Henry; Mr. Henry was recalled and was replaced by the present minister. Of course, the case is different with Canada because we have only three ministers, but the doctrine is the same. They are, under international law and practice, envoys, and may be recalled at any time; there is no doubt about that.
My right hon. friend has boasted of the generosity of his government in keeping Mr. Roy in office, an old former Liberal senator. Well, Mr. Roy wTas senator before 1911; when my right hon. friend took office Mr. Roy had been working for Canada for twenty years
Supply-Miscellaneous

in a foreign country, and I think everybody will agree with me that there was no party politics on his part in receiving Canadians while there. He has been working for Canada all the time. Surely his case is a little different from that of a gentleman who migjht be appointed on the eve of a general election just to find a position for him. So far as Sir Herbert Marler is concerned I must say that I do not know whether my right hon. friend could have easily found a Canadian to go as minister to Japan. When the position was created it was very hard to find anyone to go to that country and I think Sir Herbert Marler went there from a sense of duty to his country. He sacrificed himself and he has done so well that my right hon. friend has given him something which we would not have given him, a title. The conditions are not identical with those which would surround the appointment of a minister to France to replace the present minister on the eve of a general election. I agree with my right hon. friend that the minister represents the king but he also represents the government. The king appoints the minister upon the recommendation of the government and he negotiates for the government and represents the government in everything concerning the public business of his country in the foreign country to which he is accredited. I do not want to add anything to what I have said but I am sure that my right hon. friend will not make any change under the present circumstances.

Amendment agreed to.
To provide, notwithstanding the terms of the Civil Service Act or any other act or law, for payment of honoraria to members of the public service-subject to allocation by the treasury board, $10,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) whose department is most affected by this item prefers that I should make the observations which he would desire to make. There are men in various departments of the public service who have rendered extra services to the country. Upon a former occasion the late Mr. Robb asked for an appropriation of a similar amount to provide for similar payments. In many cases these ^ men have assumed the functions of deputies. Take the case of one gentleman who will be covered by this vote, Mr. Pearson. Mr. Pearson is on the verge of a complete breakdown because of the extra work he did in connection with the price spreads commission. He worked many nights and sometimes well into -the next day. This amount is to take care of such cases and the principle

was adopted by the late Mr. Robb in dealing with exceptional conditions which arose in connection with public business.
I do not intend to take exception to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has said but I do think it is desirable that wherever possible the name of the person should be specified.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Robb did not mention names in his estimates.

Whether that was not done formerly or whether it is not being done at the present time, I think it would create a better feeling in the service generally to give full particulars of these special recommendations. In the case mentioned by the Prime Minister, I agree and I think every hon. member will agree that Mr. Pearson performed services which it would have been extremely difficult to have obtained otherwise. The mention of Mr. Pearson's name would not have made it less easy for the item to be .passed and I think it might have helped to avoid some of the feeling which is certain to arise among other members of the service where names are not specified and a general power is given.
Item agreed to.
National research council-further amount required, $100,000.

The main
estimates contained a vote of something like $400,000 for the national research council and I should like to know what has made necessary an additional amount of $100,000 within the time which has elapsed since the main estimates were before the house.

I shall
be glad to give the committee full information. As the right hon. gentleman has stated, vote No. 284 in the main estimates provided an amount of $400,000 which is necessary for existing activities but which does not permit the council effectively to discharge the duties and responsibilities assigned to it. The supplementary estimate is required for four different matters.
First, it is to provide for pressing new activities. These include the transfer to the national research council of the testing laboratories of the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario; the investigation of problems of the building and construction industry, including research on building materials; the organization of a cooperative investigation in the field of aquicuiture, limnobiology, and fresh water biology; the coordination of work on the

Supply-Research Council
extremely important problem of silicosis; and to provide for any additional new problems which may arise or which may be assigned to the council by the government.
The laboratories of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario at present fix safety standards and test electrical equipment offered for sale in Canada, and their test is accepted by the fire underwriters. There is no such laboratory in any other province, at present the manufacturers depending largely on the underwriters laboratories in the United States. It is extremely undesirable that each province should establish its own laboratory, as this would mean duplication of equipment and operating expense and would inevitably lead to a multiplicity of provincial standards governing the manufacture of electrical equipment, with increased cost to the consumer. The national research council has consequently established a national laboratory for the testing of such equipment for all of the provinces except Ontario, which has its own laboratory. It is now proposed that the national research laboratories should serve the entire dominion in this matter, and although the attorney general of Ontario was at first opposed on the ground of provincial rights, he has changed his view and the way is now clear to transfer these provincial laboratories to the control of the national research council. It is considered expedient that prompt action should be taken in this matter.
The construction industry is the third largest in Canada, but only meagre scientific data are available regarding materials and practices used in construction in the dominion. Further, the use by architects and contractors of information secured from foreign laboratories adversely affects the use of Canadian materials. Considerable sums have been provided bv the British government for research in this field and much of this valuable information might be made applicable to Canadian conditions at comparatively small expense. There is also great need for definite information regarding Canadian building materials. The Canadian Construction Association, the Royal Architectural Institute, the Canadian Hospital Council and the Canadian Manufacturers Association have all urged that the national research council undertake work in this field. The council is convinced that both the industry and the public would benefit greatly by such work and that the expenditure would be extremely small compared to the benefits to be derived. This work is extremely important at a time when Canada is planning considerable expenditure on a housing plan.
Second, this vote is to provide grants in aid of research and also to provide for applications received during the coming year. During the four years, 1928 to 1932, the average annual expenditure of the national research council on grants in aid of research in laboratories throughout Canada totalled approximately $140,000. Owing to increased commitments in connection with the establishment of the national research laboratories, combined with a reduced appropriation, the council was able to allocate only S5.000 for this purpose this year, from its existing appropriation. It is therefore considered essential that this small additional amount be provided in order that the council may in some measure discharge its obligation to stimulate research work throughout Canada.
Third, it is to provide for general administration, including increased amounts required for the operation of the laboratories and publication, also for travelling expenses of council members, staff and members of associate committees with the object of coordinating and directing research work on main cooperative projects. For the purpose of coordinating and directing cooperative investigations on major research problems the national research council has in active operation more than twenty-five associate committees with a total membership of several hundred eminent scientists and business men, who are serving without remuneration in directing and carrying on this work. It is necessary that these committees should meet at reasonable intervals to report and discuss past work and future activities. The council has been able to provide for this purpose only $2,400 from its existing appropriation. It is clear that these committees cannot function efficiently unless this appropriation is increased.
It has been necessary for the appropriations for the operation of the national research laboratories to be reduced below the amount provided last year by $3,500, and it is considered essential that this allotment be increased in the interest of efficient operation.
It is also necessary that the allotment for the publication of the Canadian Journal of Research be increased to provide for the publication of the results of researches undertaken in the national research laboratories and in other Canadian laboratories. It is essential that the results of the researches carried on should be made available by publication.
Fourth, the vote is to provide equipment urgently required by the national research laboratories. More than $185,000 actually
Supply-Research Council

voted by parliament for equipment in the national research laboratories remained unexpended at the end of the year 1932-33. This equipment was urgently required but it was considered necessary to effect this saving, owing to the serious financial situation then existing. However, it was understood that necessary equipment would be provided in instalments from year to year, and in fulfilment of this understanding the sum of $25,000 was voted in 1933-34 and $30,000 in 1934-35. Therefore, of the amount voted by parliament in 1932-33 for equipment in the national research laboratories, there remains unexpended, at the present time, more than $133,000. They take the view that this amount has been standing to their credit, and they are asking to have a portion voted this year.
Does the minister think that the financial situation has improved since 1932?

I certainly do. The national research council requests that part of these unexpended moneys previously provided by parliament for this purpose be voted this year to provide equipment urgently required in order effectively to carry on the work of the council. A detailed statement of equipment required by the council can be given if desired. The vote requested will be used for the purchase and installation of equipment listed and also such other equipment as may be necessary for the effective prosecution of new projects undertaken by the council.

Item agreed to.
Governor General's Warrants, 1934-35
Expenses of the royal commission on price spreads and mass buying (governor general's warrants of July 30, November 3, and December 10, 1934). $155,000.
What was the total cost of this investigation?

The hon. gentleman will recall that part of it was under a committee of the house last year and part of it under a royal commission. The actual cost of the two was in the vicinity of $475,000 plus some printing, the actual amount of which I have never been able to get. I do not know that my department is specifically responsible for checking the matter because it did not come through us. The first part was entirely a House of Commons matter
rMr. R. B. Hanson.]
and was in last year's vote, but my understanding is that the actual cost of the whole, including the printing, which of course is under the printing bureau, was about $475,000. It may be a little more or a little less.
A half million, in round figures.
A little less.

There was a rumour among the commissioners-I -could never trace it- that the government succeeded in collecting arrears of taxes from certain corporations. Will the minister make a statement in that regard?
We do not generally deal in rumours, but I have it on good authority that as the result of the activities of the commission there was turned into the coffers of the country a very Large sum of money.
Large enough to pay all the expenses of the commission?
It is a matter of rumour; the money was not paid to me, so I do not know.
I believe this question was asked the Minister of Finance not long ago and he said there was not.

I asked the Minister of National Revenue that question on March 12, 1935. The question and answer were as follows:
Mr. Golding: Have any sums been collected by the income tax departments as a result of revelations before the price spreads and mass buying commission, and if so what is the amount?
Mr. Matthews:	I am informed that the
answer is no; no amount has been collected.
That is four months ago.

If any sum has been collected the committee ought to have that information. This investigation has cost the country a lot of money and I would call the attention of the house to the fact that when 'the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) proposed a resolution asking for an investigation into the spread between the price received by producers and the price paid by consumers for certain goods and agricultural commodities-that resolution was

Supply-Governor General's Warrants
brought in on February 6, 1933-he suggested that the investigation be made through the research council. In view of the enormous expense in connection with this affair, I think that wa9 a very wise suggestion; and had it been acted on the same information could have been obtained at a fraction of the cost. Hon. gentlemen should pay some attention to the statements that- have been made inregard to the questions that were answered. Take some of the witnesses who were brought heTe. It is interesting to take the report of the proceedings and read the evidence given, by these witnesses, and then, to reflect upon the expense involved in bringing them here. We find that one witness coming from the west and giving evidence was paid-this was part of one day-S149.15, and it would not have required more -than a three cent postage stamp to secure from him all the information he gave. About all he did in a constructive way was ,to recommend that we should1 have a policy of inflation, and that is what we have had to a certain extent. Another witness brought down cost $150 or a little over, and the only constructive suggestions he offered were these two: first, that the farmer should not sell any of his products on the farm, and secondly, that we ought to have hogs graded on the rail, which has been in effect for some time, in Ontario at any rate, where it is optional. I should like this same gentleman to go to the farmers of Ontario'and tell them they should not sell anything on their farms; I fancy he would not get a very good reception. But the point is -that that evidence cost over $150, whereas all that was needed was a three cent postage stamp-and you would not have needed that.
I do not think the price spreads commission finished their work at all, because in my opinion they should have investigated some of the prices in connection with the commission itself. This was a price spreads investigating commission, and we have Mr. Sommerville receiving $150 a day and $15 expenses, and Mr. Parry receiving $35 a day and $15 expenses. I think they should have had an investigation there to find out the reason for this spread between these two prices. Further, Mr. Sommerville was paid for 196 days while the committee and the commission sat for only 124 days; in other words, he was paid for 72 days when neither the committee nor the commission was sitting at all.
Including Sundays?

No; I checked that. I asked some questions in regard to this matter. The first was:
How many days did Norman Sommerville, K.C., act as counsel for the committee and royal commission on price spreads and mass buying?
The answer was this:
Mr. Norman Sommerville, K.C., acted as counsel for the committee and the royal commission on price spreads and mass buying for 196 days; 124 days of this period were spent in actually attending public sessions of the committee and the commission, while the balance of 72 days was devoted to interviewing witnesses-
Mark you!
-consultations with auditors, investigators, and in preparing the evidence to be adduced before the committee or commission.
The second question was:
What was his remuneration per day?
The answer was:
Mr. Sommerville's remuneration was $150 per day for the above period. This rate of remuneration was authorized by the committee and later confirmed by the commission. During the summer Mr. Sommerville-
Listen to this.

devoted a considerable amount of time to the gathering and preparation of evidence for submission to the commission, to consultations with auditors and investigators, and to interviewing of witnesses, but for this work no account was submitted and no remuneration paid.
The answer to the first question told us that for those seventy-two days when neither the committee nor the commission was sitting, he was paid, and it gave what he was doing during that time, namely, interviewing witnesses and having consultations with auditors and investigators. In the answer to the next question we are told that he was doing that during the summer and was not paid at all for that work.
Was that not in addition?

I can quite understand that may be the interpretation of the answer, but I was under the impression that this was an investigation, not a prosecution; and what I and the country would like to know is why those witnesses were approached, interviewed and no doubt consulted and prompted before they came before the committee or the commission.

Supply-Governor General's Warrants
Be careful.

I have not any doubt
that is what happened. My opinion-and I think this is the opinion of the people generally-is that those witnesses should have come before the committee or commission without any interference whatsoever and given their evidence. Furthermore, we find a list of witnesses that were paid and a large number of witnesses that were not paid at all. If this was an investigation and the whole object was to ascertain the facts and the truth of the situation, one witness ought to be paid just as well as another; I think that is a fair submission. We have the spread between the fees Mr. Parry and Mr. Sommer-ville were paid. I would like to ask the minister this: What did the firm of auditors, Clarkson, Gordon, Dilworth, Guilfoyle and Nash put in for the services of their auditors per individual per day? That is the first question.

Without
questioning the hon. gentleman's right to discuss this matter at all under this vote-
Why mention it?

If the
hon. gentleman will allow me to continue, perhaps I can make the position clear; I do not know that it calls for any interruption at all. I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman and the committee that the expenditures of the house committee and of the royal commission were not under the control of any department of government, and the information, if it is necessary, ought to be sought from the committee or the royal commission itself. We had no control over the amount paid to witnesses or to counsel-
No?

Well, the
auditor general may have had some control, but I understand that in every case the committee voted the money; it was our duty to pay it and it was paid. So far as I am concerned, as minister of this department, I assume no responsibility for what the committee did in the way of expenditures. The house voted the money and it is a responsibility of every member of the house just as much as it is of the government. As regards the amount paid to the auditors, which of course was very large, I do not know how the amount was distributed to any particular

individual. That is not the way in which these services are charged for by an auditing firm. They do a job and charge a sum. No doubt the items for the auditors' work came before the committee; the committee must have thought they were satisfactory because my understanding is that the committee unanimously voted to pay these bills.

The
question is not whether the committee did so; the point is that we are entitled to receive the information and the minister can get it from the auditor general who must have audited all these vouchers and receipts. Surely when an hon. member asks for information, he 'is entitled to receive it.

If I had
had any notice that this matter w'as coming up-

Get the information
to-morrow.
I shall be glad to get whatever information is available, but as a matter of fact the Department of Trade and Commerce had no responsibility for the expenditure.

I quite
appreciate that, but the House of Commons is entitled to the information.

May I as a member of the committee say that we were never consulted about the auditors' bills. The amount of , the counsel fee was fixed by the committee and the commission, but the fees of the auditors were never submitted to the committee or the commission. I do not know yet how they were fixed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The accounts were rendered to the committee and the commission and certified, and the auditor general paid them.
They were never submitted to the committee or commission for approval.
I want to thank the minister because I think he is fair. He has not the information.

Will the minister bring the information to-morrow?
Progress reported.
